content: On September 15–18, 2020, the Guideline Development Group (GDG), led by two co-chairs and supported by the WHO Steering Group and a guideline methodologist, utilized a structured decision-making framework. This framework was the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, specifically designed for public health interventions. The framework considered several factors, including the priority of the problem, the balance of benefits and harms of the intervention, the certainty of the evidence, the value placed on outcomes by those affected, the intervention's impact on equity, resource implications, and the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention. The WHO Steering Group prepared a set of null recommendations, which included both for and against options as a neutral starting point for GDG discussions during the September 2020 meeting. Systematic review teams, in collaboration with the guideline methodologist and the WHO Steering Group, populated the EtD framework with data from systematic reviews and other sources. These reviews, along with GRADE evidence profiles and the null recommendations, were shared with the GDG before the meeting to form the basis of their discussions. The GDG formulated either strong or conditional recommendations for or against each intervention or group of interventions based on the evidence of benefits, harms, and other considerations within the EtD framework. A strong recommendation indicated that the GDG was confident that the desirable effects of adhering to the recommendation outweighed the undesirable effects. In such cases, most informed patients would choose the recommended intervention, and policymakers could adopt it as a policy in most situations. Conversely, a conditional recommendation suggested that the desirable effects probably outweighed the undesirable effects, but with less confidence. In these cases, patient choices might vary based on individual values and preferences, and shared decision-making with healthcare providers might be necessary. In addition to recommendations for managing chronic pain in children, the guidelines included a set of guiding principles approved by the GDG. These principles, rooted in human rights and ethical considerations, underpin all aspects of chronic pain management in children. As these principles are based on ethical and human rights standards, they do not require systematic reviews of research evidence on benefits and harms. The guidelines also included best practice statements, which are based on good clinical or public health practice and experience. These statements do not require systematic reviews of evidence and are generally uncontested, as failing to implement them would be nonsensical or illogical. Following the GDG meeting, the guideline writer drafted the guidelines. After approval by delegated WHO technical officers, the draft was circulated to the GDG for review and approval. The draft final guideline was also sent for peer review by the External Review Group (ERG). The role of peer review was to provide technical feedback, identify factual errors, comment on language clarity, and offer considerations related to implementation, adaptation, and contextual issues. Peer reviewers did not alter the recommendations agreed upon by the GDG, but major concerns, if identified, could be referred back to the GDG. In this case, no such concerns arose. WHO has an internal approval and quality assurance process to ensure that all its publications, including guidelines, meet the highest international standards for quality, reporting, and presentation. These guidelines were reviewed and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) and senior WHO leadership, including the Deputy Director-General and Chief Scientist. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in the pharmacological, physical, and psychological management of chronic pain in children, particularly for areas where the certainty of evidence was low or very low. Unless new evidence necessitates an earlier review, the guidelines will be systematically reviewed five years after publication. The Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing at WHO headquarters in Geneva, along with internal partners, will conduct systematic reviews of relevant evidence and assess the need for updating or revalidating the guidelines. Stakeholder input will be sought on the scope of the updated guidelines as new interventions and considerations emerge.
